lead: Coherent receivers need a carrier phase reference. In many links the phase is unknown or drifts, because the receiver oscillator is not locked to the transmitter. Non-coherent detection avoids phase recovery. For FSK and OOK it uses envelope detectors. For PSK it encodes data in phase changes and detects those changes with a one-bit delay (DPSK). The price is a small loss in error probability. These schemes give simple, robust receivers for low-cost wireless links, optical links and legacy data systems.
prereq: You need: 6.1 ASK and FSK, 6.2 BPSK, and the matched-filter and decision-region ideas from Unit 5.

blocks.text: Non-coherent detection means the receiver does not know the carrier phase. It uses only the envelope, the slowly varying amplitude of the bandpass signal. The envelope is non-negative. A phase reversal does not change it.

For binary FSK (BFSK), bit 1 is a tone at f<sub>1</sub> and bit 0 is a tone at f<sub>2</sub>. The receiver has two bandpass filters, one at each frequency. Each filter output goes to an envelope detector. A comparator decides 1 when the f<sub>1</sub> envelope is larger and 0 otherwise. The tones must be orthogonal. The minimum spacing for non-coherent orthogonal BFSK is 1/T<sub>b</sub>, where T<sub>b</sub> is the bit duration in seconds. This is twice the coherent spacing 1/(2T<sub>b</sub>).

blocks.where: P<sub>b</sub> is bit error probability; E<sub>b</sub> is received energy per bit in joules; N<sub>0</sub> is the AWGN power spectral density in W/Hz. This is for orthogonal non-coherent BFSK.

blocks.text: Non-coherent OOK sends bit 1 as a carrier burst and bit 0 as silence. A bandpass filter, envelope detector and threshold recover the bit. The same error form applies, with E<sub>b</sub> the energy of the on burst. The threshold must be set from the noise level, not from a phase reference.

items: Filter the received signal at f<sub>1</sub> and at f<sub>2</sub>.
Compare the two envelopes at the end of the bit.
Decide the larger envelope; no phase reference is used.

blocks.text: DPSK is differential phase shift keying. Some syllabi call DPSK differential phase shift keying. It avoids absolute phase recovery by making each transmitted phase depend on the current bit and the previous transmitted phase.

blocks.where: b<sub>k</sub> is the input bit at time k; d<sub>k</sub> is the encoded bit; d<sub>k−1</sub> is the previous encoded bit; ⊕ is XOR. The receiver knows the initial reference d<sub>0</sub>.

blocks.text: A BPSK modulator maps d<sub>k</sub> = 1 to phase 180° and d<sub>k</sub> = 0 to phase 0° (or the opposite convention). With this convention, the phase change from bit k−1 to k is 180° when b<sub>k</sub> = 1 and 0° when b<sub>k</sub> = 0. The absolute phase may drift; the change over one bit carries the data.

items: Split the received signal into a direct path and a delayed path.
Delay one copy by exactly T<sub>b</sub>.
Multiply the direct signal by the delayed copy.
Threshold the filtered product at the end of the bit to recover the phase change.

blocks.where: P<sub>b</sub> is bit error probability; E<sub>b</sub> is energy per bit in joules; N<sub>0</sub> is AWGN power spectral density in W/Hz. This is a high-SNR approximation for DPSK in AWGN.

blocks.text: DPSK is slightly worse than coherent BPSK at the same Eb/N0; coherent BPSK is in 6.2. DPSK needs no carrier recovery, so it tolerates slow phase drift. Fast phase noise changes the phase over one bit and raises errors; treat this effect qualitatively.
The three non-coherent options differ in what they assume and what they cost.

items: Non-coherent BFSK: no phase reference; tone spacing 1/T<sub>b</sub>; P<sub>b</sub> = ½ exp(−E<sub>b</sub>/(2N<sub>0</sub>)).
Non-coherent OOK: no phase reference; one threshold; same P<sub>b</sub> form as BFSK.
DPSK: no absolute phase; one-bit delay; P<sub>b</sub> ≈ ½ exp(−E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>).
Coherent BPSK: needs carrier recovery; best binary error probability; see 6.2.

blocks.text: Non-coherent BFSK suits low-cost sensor links and simple telemetry. OOK suits very cheap on-off remote modules. DPSK suits links with phase drift and a simple delay detector, such as some optical and wireless systems. M-ary non-coherent schemes are in 6.5; fading is in 6.9.
In a phone link the phase can spin because of oscillator offset. A non-coherent receiver still works if the phase is constant over one bit; DPSK assumes exactly that.

figure.caption: DPSK sends differentially encoded bits through a BPSK modulator; the receiver multiplies the signal by a copy delayed by one bit T<sub>b</sub>, lowpass filters the product and thresholds it.

spec.title: DPSK transmitter and delay detector
spec.aria: Data is differentially encoded, modulated, sent through a channel, split into a direct path and a one-bit delay, multiplied, lowpass filtered and thresholded.

examples.question: A DPSK system uses the rule d<sub>k</sub> = b<sub>k</sub> ⊕ d<sub>k−1</sub> with initial d<sub>0</sub> = 0. The input bit stream is 1 1 0 1. Find the encoded bits d<sub>k</sub> and the phase changes if bit 1 gives 180° and bit 0 gives 0°.
steps: Phase changes follow b: b = 1 1 0 1 gives 180°, 180°, 0°, 180°.
examples.answer: Encoded bits d = 1 0 0 1; phase changes are 180°, 180°, 0°, 180°.
examples.check:
b = [1, 1, 0, 1]
d_prev = 0
d = []
ph = []
for x in b:
    y = x ^ d_prev
    d.append(y)
    ph.append(180 if x == 1 else 0)
    d_prev = y
for v in d:
    print(v)
for v in ph:
    print(v)

traps: Forgetting d<sub>0</sub>: DPSK encoding needs an initial reference bit, fixed and known at the receiver.
Using the coherent BPSK formula Q(√(2E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>)) for DPSK. Use P<sub>b</sub> ≈ ½ exp(−E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>).
Using tone spacing 1/(2T<sub>b</sub>) for non-coherent BFSK. Non-coherent orthogonal BFSK needs 1/T<sub>b</sub>.
Mixing the exponents: non-coherent BFSK and OOK have E<sub>b</sub>/(2N<sub>0</sub>); DPSK has E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>.
Reading DPSK phase changes as absolute phases. The data is in the change between adjacent bits, not in one phase alone.

quiz.q: State the rule for non-coherent BFSK detection.
quiz.a: Filter the signal at the two tone frequencies, envelope-detect each filter output, and decide the bit from the larger envelope.

quiz.q: Why can an envelope detector ignore the carrier phase?
quiz.a: The envelope is the magnitude of the bandpass signal. A phase reversal changes the signed carrier but not its magnitude, so the envelope detector output is unchanged.

quiz.q: A non-coherent BFSK system has T<sub>b</sub> = 1 ms. Find the minimum orthogonal tone spacing.
DPSK uses d<sub>k</sub> = b<sub>k</sub> ⊕ d<sub>k−1</sub> with d<sub>0</sub> = 0. Encode the bits 0 1 1.
quiz.a: d<sub>1</sub> = 0 ⊕ 0 = 0; d<sub>2</sub> = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1; d<sub>3</sub> = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0. Encoded bits are 0 1 0.

quiz.q: At the same E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>, which has lower P<sub>b</sub>: DPSK or coherent BPSK? Why?
quiz.a: Coherent BPSK has lower P<sub>b</sub>. DPSK compares a noisy received signal with a noisy delayed copy, so it is slightly worse than coherent BPSK at the same E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>.

quiz.q: Why does non-coherent BFSK need 1/T<sub>b</sub> spacing rather than 1/(2T<sub>b</sub>)?
quiz.a: With unknown phase, the two tones must be orthogonal for every possible phase difference. The inner product over one bit then vanishes only when the spacing is an integer multiple of 1/T<sub>b</sub>; the minimum is 1/T<sub>b</sub>.

quiz.q: For DPSK with E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> = 8, estimate P<sub>b</sub>.
Give the P<sub>b</sub> formula for non-coherent orthogonal BFSK.

beyond: Not for the exam. DPSK appears in optical links as differential phase modulation with delay interferometers, and in simple wireless links where carrier recovery is costly. Modern systems often use pilot symbols or coherent detection with digital phase tracking. Non-coherent FSK remains in low-power telemetry and some pager and RFID systems. Search next for differential detection, phase noise, non-coherent FSK and optical DPSK.
